slides.sub: What Bitcoin is, what it is made of, and why every part of it exists
slides.notes: Mastering Bitcoin, 3rd edition, chapter 1, Introduction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023), free under CC BY-SA 4.0. This deck follows the chapter's own concept taxonomy: 90 concepts in 6 branches, of which 42 carry a worked example. Every number, hash, address and output on these slides was executed under Python 3.14.4 by the chapter's own examples and checked against the figure the chapter corpus records; the deck is refused by its checker if any of them stops agreeing.

slides.title: One chapter, six branches

slides.notes:
SAY: Chapter 1 begins by saying that Bitcoin is a collection of concepts and technologies that form the basis of a digital money ecosystem, and that units of currency called bitcoin are used to store and transmit value among the participants of the Bitcoin network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: One bitcoin divides into 100 million satoshis

slides.notes:
SAY: The Unit section answers the first question that any money raises, namely what the money is called and in what pieces it is counted. It contains the name of the currency, with its distinction between the unit and the system, and the smallest subdivision that can be recorded, the satoshi.
ASK: How many satoshis buy a coffee at today's price?
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 1 - Unit.
slides.take: Money here is counting, and the units are exact

slides.title: 21 million, by rule - not by promise
slides.sub: Issuance halves every 210,000 blocks; the cap is the sum

items.title: Block subsidy per era of 210,000 blocks (BTC)

items.label: the sum of every era's issuance

slides.notes:
SAY: The Supply section is about how much bitcoin exists and how the amount grows. The chapter says that the protocol periodically decreases the number of new bitcoins that are created, limiting the total to a fixed number just below 21 million, so that the number in circulation follows a predictable curve (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
ASK: Why does the sum stop just short of 21 million?
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 1 - Supply, Issuance.
slides.take: Scarcity is enforced by arithmetic every node checks

SAY: The Price section addresses a question that every newcomer asks, namely who sets the price of bitcoin. The chapter's short answer is that the price is set by markets (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

slides.title: Network
slides.sub: No bank in the middle - and what replaces it
slides.notes:
SAY: The Network branch is about the community of computers that runs Bitcoin and the way it agrees on a single history without a leader. The chapter describes Bitcoin as a distributed, peer-to-peer system in which there is no central server or point of control, and as a protocol, a peer-to-peer network, and a distributed computing innovation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 1 - Network.

slides.title: Wallets and first use
slides.sub: Choosing software, holding keys, and the first payment
slides.notes:
SAY: A wallet is the software through which a person uses Bitcoin. The chapter calls the Bitcoin wallet the most common user interface to the Bitcoin system, just as a web browser is the most common user interface for the protocol of the web, and the glossary of the book describes it as software that holds your Bitcoin addresses and secret keys and lets you send, receive and store your bitcoin (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 1 - Wallet, Usage.

slides.title: Foundations
slides.sub: The two old problems Bitcoin finally joined up
slides.notes:
SAY: The Foundations branch collects the general technical ideas that the rest of the chapter takes for granted. Chapter 1 of the textbook introduces Bitcoin through a story about Alice and Joe, and in doing so it uses words such as digital signature, private key, blockchain, node, protocol and QR code as if every reader already knew them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 1 - Foundations.

slides.title: Two solved problems, one new system
slides.sub: 1997 and 1982 meet in 2008

items.head: Hashcash (1997)
items.body: Proof-of-work: make sending cost a computation, so flooding costs real resources. Bitcoin turns the same cost into the price of writing history.

items.head: Byzantine Generals (1982)
items.body: How do parties that cannot trust each other agree on one message? Proof-of-work plus the longest valid chain is Bitcoin's practical answer.

slides.take: Bitcoin's novelty is the combination, not the parts

slides.title: From keys to the chain
slides.sub: The pipeline the rest of the course walks

items: Each stage only trusts what it can verify
Every later chapter opens one of these boxes

slides.notes:
SAY: The Chain section explains the data structure at the centre of Bitcoin and the computers that maintain it. The block is a group of transactions that the network accepts together, the blockchain is the list of blocks linked one to the next, the timestamp is the mark of time that orders them, and the node is a computer that takes part in the network.
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 1 - Chain, Cryptography.
slides.take: This pipeline is the course syllabus in one row

slides.sub: Each block carries the digest of the one before

slides.notes:
SAY: The Computing section explains the ordinary technology on which Bitcoin software runs and by which people reach it. It covers the internet and the rules that computers follow on it, the way programs talk to each other through interfaces, the way data is named and stored, the operating systems and browsers in which wallets live, and the units in which computers count.
